abstract: An inhibitory autoreceptor distributed across serotonin neurons in the raphe nuclei, hippocampus, and limbic cortex. On raphe neurons it suppresses serotonergic firing; at postsynaptic sites it dampens limbic excitability and supports mood stability. Reduced 5-HT1A activity is associated with baseline anxiety, irritability, and low mood resilience.
presentation: A calm baseline; under-function surfaces as free-floating anxiety and low resilience to stress.
effect: Inhibitory: lowers cAMP, opens potassium channels
body: Tonic postsynaptic 5-HT1A activity in the hippocampus and limbic cortex maintains a stable affective baseline: when receptor activity is adequate, anxiety is low and mood responds proportionately to stressors; when it falls, vigilance and irritability predominate. Somatodendritic 5-HT1A receptors on raphe neurons function as autoreceptors, suppressing serotonin release through negative feedback and shaping the depth and duration of serotonergic signaling across the brain. Activation of postsynaptic 5-HT1A receptors in prefrontal cortex inhibit GABA interneurons leading to increased release of dopamine, acetylcholine, and norepinephrine downstream.

abstract: Highly expressed on cortical pyramidal neurons, 5-HT2A modulates perceptual gain and emotional salience. At physiological levels it heightens sensory contrast and reinforces a coherent sense of self; excessive agonism can dissolve ego boundaries and produce the hallucinations and sensory distortions characteristic of the psychedelic state. Antagonism at this receptor reduces cortical excitability, which is the basis of how several antipsychotics attenuate hallucination.
presentation: Tonic 5-HT2A drives cortical excitability and perceptual clarity; agonism opens altered perception and vivid imagery; over-function surfaces as hallucination and ego dissolution.
effect: Excitatory: raises IP3 / DAG via phospholipase C
figure_caption: Fig. 2 · Excitatory Gq coupling, cortical pyramidal neuron
body: At physiological serotonin concentrations, 5-HT2A promotes cortical arousal and sharpens perceptual salience. When driven well beyond its normal operating range (by exogenous agonists or in certain pathological states), sensory boundaries break down: the sense of self loosens, and ordinary stimuli can acquire overwhelming meaning or give way to frank hallucination. Antagonism reduces cortical excitability and attenuates perceptual distortion, which accounts for much of the antipsychotic effect of agents that block it. The receptor also shapes sleep architecture; excessive activity fragments slow-wave sleep.

abstract: Tonic 5-HT2C activity restrains mesolimbic dopamine outflow and promotes satiety through hypothalamic signalling, providing a dual check on appetite and reward-seeking. Loss of this restraint is associated with escalating hunger, weight gain, and disinhibited appetitive drive.
presentation: Adequate 5-HT2C activity promotes satiety and limits reward-seeking; reduced tone is associated with persistent appetite and disinhibited approach behaviour.
effect: Excitatory (Gq); excites circuits that suppress appetite and, via GABAergic relays, restrain mesolimbic dopamine
body: When active, 5-HT2C exerts a tonic brake on mesolimbic dopamine release and signals satiation to the hypothalamus, providing a dual check on hunger and appetitive drive. When this restraint is reduced, appetite increases and reward-seeking becomes less inhibited, contributing to the weight gain associated with medications that block 5-HT2C. Its influence on mood is less direct, mediated through the same appetite and interoceptive circuits.

abstract: A ligand-gated cation channel on vagal afferents and the area postrema, 5-HT3 activation triggers nausea, retching, and vomiting. It is serotonin's only ionotropic receptor and a clinically relevant target at the intersection of gut-brain signalling, mood, and gastrointestinal distress.
presentation: Activation triggers visceral alarm: nausea, retching, and vomiting; blockade silences this signal and reduces gut-brain crosstalk.
effect: Fast excitatory: opens a cation channel (emesis)
body: 5-HT3 is serotonin's only fast ionotropic receptor, a pentameric cation channel structurally related to nicotinic and GABA-A receptors. It is expressed on vagal afferents and in the area postrema, the brainstem's chemoreceptor trigger zone, where serotonin release activates it to produce nausea, retching, and vomiting. Antagonism blocks this signal and is the basis of 5-HT3 receptor antiemetics. Its role in cortical circuits is less well characterised, but it may modulate mood and cognition through interoceptive pathways.

abstract: SERT terminates serotonergic transmission by sodium-coupled reuptake, controlling the duration and spread of every serotonergic signal; it is the target of the most widely used class of antidepressants, SSRIs, and its causal role in depression itself remains disputed.
presentation: A brisk pump sets a brief serotonergic pulse and lower mood baseline; blockade extends each signal and lifts resilience to stress.
body: SERT clears serotonin from the synapse, determining the half-life of each serotonergic signal. By mediating reuptake of 5-HT (serotonin) into presynaptic neurons, SERT regulates serotinergic signaling throughout the brain. Due to interactions with other key cerebral molecules and its contribution to neurotransmission, SERT plays an integral role in the pathophysiology of depression. Activity and expression of SERT is regulated by pro-inflammatory cytokines and growth factors which then affects serotonin transmission and neural plasticity. Other influencers of SERT function include environmental exposure, diet, gut microbiota, and therapy. Genetic variations in the SLC6A4 gene influence the expression and function of SERT which leads to differences in depression symptoms as well as treatment response.

abstract: D1 activity follows an inverted-U relationship with performance: insufficient tone impairs sustained firing in task-relevant circuits, while excess dopamine produces disordered, noisy activity. Both extremes can manifest as the cognitive and negative dimensions of thought disorder.
presentation: At optimal tone: crisp working memory, sustained focus, and orderly cognition. Off the peak: distractibility, disorganization, racing or stalled thought, and the blunting and poverty of thought that underlie the cognitive dimension of psychosis.
body: D1 is the dominant dopamine receptor in the prefrontal cortex, where it sustains signal in task-relevant circuits. The relationship between D1 stimulation and cognitive performance is non-linear: insufficient dopamine impairs the persistent firing that working memory requires, while excess dopamine drives haphazard, disorganised activity. In schizophrenia, the negative and cognitive symptoms (flat affect, alogia, avolition, poor working memory) are linked to insufficient prefrontal D1 tone; disorganised thought and positive symptoms track more closely with NMDA hypofunction and mesolimbic dopamine excess than with the prefrontal D1 curve itself.

abstract: The dopamine receptor that governs its own transmitter's supply. D2 sits presynaptically on midbrain dopamine neurons, where it slows firing and suppresses release, and postsynaptically on the striatal projection neurons of the indirect pathway. What deviates at D2 is dopamine availability rather than the receptor itself, which is why it is at once the most heavily occupied target in psychiatric pharmacology and an unconvincing site of primary pathology.
body: D2 receptors describe a class of dopamine receptors with inhibitory activty. They are located presynaptically on dopaminegic neurons where they are the primary regulators of dopamine release through negative feedback. D2 receptors can also be found on postsynaptically on non-dopamine neurons, thought to function as regulators of neuronal activity in other neutrotransmitter pathways. The regulating activity of D2 receptors controls dopamine release in the mesocorticolimbic and striatonigral systems. Striatal Dopamine D2 receptors regulate reward and salience signals D2 receptor activity in the mesolimbic pathway plays imporatn role in emotionally-motivated behaviors such as motivation, reward, and pleasure.

abstract: Concentrated in the limbic striatum, D3 modulates motivation and the drive to pursue reward. Reduced activity is associated with anhedonia and amotivation, in which goals lose urgency and reward loses salience. Excessive agonism disrupts impulse control, producing compulsive behaviour patterns including pathological gambling and hypersexuality.
presentation: Underfunction: anhedonia (nothing feels rewarding or worth the effort), amotivation, and flat drive; things that should feel compelling instead feel empty. Overfunction: heightened wanting, compulsive pursuit, and impulse dyscontrol, producing the compulsive patterns seen in gambling, hypersexuality, and binge eating.
body: When D3 activity is within its normal range, it supports goal-directed behaviour and reward anticipation. Reduced activity impairs motivational drive; clinically this presents as anhedonia and the negative symptoms of amotivation and blunted affect. Excessive D3 signalling, conversely, impairs behavioural inhibition, contributing to the impulse control disorders seen particularly with D2/D3 agonism in Parkinson's disease. Its predominantly limbic distribution means D3 can in principle be targeted for motivational symptoms with a lower risk of the extrapyramidal effects associated with nigrostriatal D2 antagonism.

abstract: DAT clears dopamine from the synapse, determining the kinetics of dopaminergic signalling. A slow, gradual rise in dopamine sustains attention and supports goal-directed action; a rapid, large surge activates the reward circuit powerfully and stamps in reinforcement. DAT is concentrated in the striatum, the core circuit of learned association and craving.
presentation: Rapid surges: euphoria, craving, and compulsive seeking. Gradual occupancy: sustained focus, improved attention, and the measured pace of goal-pursuit without the spike of reinforcement that drives addiction.
body: The rate of dopamine rise and its duration determine whether a signal functions as reinforcement or as sustained tone. An abrupt, large surge activates the mesolimbic reward circuit intensely: the synapse encodes that this context is predictive of reward, and the experience is accompanied by craving and compulsive seeking. A slow, measured increase in dopamine (as with extended-release formulations) occupies the same receptors without producing that discrete reinforcement signal, supporting attention and goal pursuit without driving compulsive behaviour. The prefrontal cortex expresses relatively little DAT, so blockade there has limited effect on dopamine clearance; the striatum is where transporter occupancy most directly shapes reinforcement and craving.

abstract: An excitatory adrenergic receptor that drives arousal and vascular tone. Centrally, high activity feeds hyperarousal, trauma nightmares, and fragmented sleep; its blockade quiets those hyperadrenergic surges. Peripherally, it tightens blood vessels; its blockade causes dizziness on standing and sedation.
presentation: Central excess: hyperarousal, fragmented sleep, trauma nightmares; peripheral loss: light-headedness on standing, drowsiness.
body: Central α1 activity sustains arousal and underlies the hypervigilance and nocturnal awakenings associated with excessive noradrenergic tone. Blockade reduces these hyperadrenergic surges, attenuating pathological startle and sleep fragmentation. Peripherally, α1 maintains vascular tone against gravitational pooling; blockade reduces this support, producing orthostatic hypotension and sedation as central arousal is dampened.

abstract: A presynaptic autoreceptor that limits norepinephrine release at the synapse and modulates prefrontal dopamine. Engaging it lowers arousal and tightens focus; releasing it raises vigilance and impulsivity. Blockade also disinhibits serotonin release, which contributes to effects on mood and energy.
presentation: Engagement: calm, steady focus, low startle, reduced heart rate and blood pressure; release: heightened alertness, impulsive drive, restlessness.
body: As a presynaptic autoreceptor, α2 senses synaptic norepinephrine and suppresses further release, reducing whole-body sympathetic tone. Agonism produces reduced startle, lower heart rate and blood pressure, and in the prefrontal cortex, improved signal-to-noise ratio that tightens sustained focus and working memory. Antagonism does the opposite, raising noradrenergic output and disinhibiting serotonin release, which accounts for the activating and mood-elevating effects of α2 blockade.

abstract: The adrenergic receptor mediating the peripheral somatic signs of sympathetic activation: tachycardia, tremor, and diaphoresis. Blockade attenuates these physical manifestations of anxiety while leaving cognitive worry largely intact, producing a calmer physiological state without sedation.
presentation: Excessive activity: pounding heart, tremor, sweating, rapid pulse; blockade: steady heartbeat, dry palms, reduced physical anxiety.
body: β-adrenergic activation produces the peripheral features of acute anxiety and fear: tachycardia, tremor, and sweating. Blockade attenuates these somatic signs; heart rate steadies and tremor diminishes, though cognitive anxiety is not directly addressed by peripheral blockade. Centrally, β-adrenergic signalling participates in the consolidation of emotionally charged memories, which has made these receptors a subject of investigation in trauma reconsolidation research, though clinical translation has been difficult.

abstract: The transporter responsible for norepinephrine clearance from the synapse, setting baseline noradrenergic tone and energy level. In the prefrontal cortex it also clears dopamine, so blockade raises prefrontal dopamine alongside norepinephrine, sharpening sustained attention. Insufficient noradrenergic tone is associated with fatigue and poor attention; excess produces restlessness.
presentation: Blockade: lifted mood and energy, sharper focus, steadier attention; underactivity: fatigue, inattention, low drive.
body: NET activity determines noradrenergic tone by setting the rate of synaptic norepinephrine clearance. Because the prefrontal cortex expresses little dopamine transporter, NET is the principal mechanism for dopamine reuptake there; blockade therefore raises prefrontal dopamine alongside norepinephrine, improving signal-to-noise in working memory circuits. Increased noradrenergic and prefrontal dopaminergic tone improves energy, sustained attention, and executive function; insufficient tone is associated with fatigue, attentional drift, and reduced drive.

abstract: The coincidence detector that underlies memory formation and synaptic plasticity. This glutamate-gated channel opens only when the cell is already depolarised (a molecular AND gate), making it the gateway of long-term potentiation. Loss of its function produces dissociation, fragmented perception, and thought disorganisation that can closely mimic psychosis.
presentation: Sharp cognition and continuous experience in health; rapid shifts in mood; under loss of function, dissociation, fragmented perception, and disorganized thought.
body: NMDA is a voltage- and ligand-gated channel that opens only when glutamate is bound and the membrane is simultaneously depolarised, expelling its magnesium plug; this coincidence-detection property makes it the molecular substrate of Hebbian plasticity and long-term potentiation. Synaptic remodelling downstream of NMDA activation unfolds over hours to days, which may account for the rapid shifts in mood and perception that accompany forced opening or sustained blockade. When NMDA function is disrupted by autoimmune attack or loss-of-function mutation, the resulting syndrome can closely resemble primary psychosis: perceptual fragmentation, derealization, and disorganised thinking, consistent with the glutamate model of psychosis.

abstract: The principal mediator of fast excitatory synaptic transmission. AMPA receptor number at a given synapse is proportional to its strength; insertion and removal of receptors during synaptic plasticity underlie learning and memory. Enhanced AMPA throughput is associated with improved cognition and antidepressant effects.
presentation: In health, sharp moment-to-moment perception and rapid learning; reduced AMPA activity dulls thought and mood, clouding cognition.
effect: Fast excitatory: the workhorse of excitation
body: AMPA opens within milliseconds of glutamate binding, depolarising the postsynaptic membrane and allowing NMDA receptors to engage. The number of AMPA receptors at a synapse reflects its functional strength: long-term potentiation involves receptor insertion, long-term depression involves removal, and this trafficking is the physical mechanism of learning and memory. Enhanced AMPA throughput is linked to improved cognitive performance and antidepressant effects, likely through downstream increases in BDNF signalling and synaptic density.

abstract: The principal fast inhibitory receptor in the brain. As a ligand-gated chloride channel, GABA-A hyperpolarizes neurons and suppresses network excitability, maintaining the seizure threshold and supporting sleep. Reduced tone produces anxiety and insomnia; abrupt withdrawal can trigger tremor and seizures; progressive enhancement leads through sedation to surgical anaesthesia.
presentation: In health, easy sleep and calm wakefulness; low tone presents as anxiety, agitation, and insomnia; loss of accustomed inhibition causes tremor and seizure.
effect: Fast inhibitory: opens a chloride channel
body: GABA-A opens a chloride channel, driving the membrane potential away from the action potential threshold and reducing neuronal firing probability. Subunit composition determines regional functional specificity: α1-containing receptors predominate in circuits mediating sedation and sleep onset, while α2/α3 receptors are more important for anxiolysis. Insufficient GABA-A activity presents clinically as anxiety, agitation, and insomnia; abrupt loss of tonic inhibition, whether from drug withdrawal or autoimmune attack, can produce tremor and generalised seizures, reflecting the role of sustained inhibitory tone in maintaining the normal seizure threshold.

abstract: The metabotropic form of GABAergic inhibition: a Gi/o-coupled receptor that opens potassium channels and closes calcium channels, producing a slow, prolonged hyperpolarization that complements the fast gating of GABA-A. It relaxes muscle tone and dampens reward urgency; strong agonism produces heavy sedation and deep sleep.
presentation: Reduced muscle tension and spasticity; blunted craving and reward drive; strong activation produces profound drowsiness and deep sleep.
effect: Slow inhibitory: opens potassium, closes calcium
body: GABA-B opens potassium channels and closes calcium channels, producing a late, prolonged phase of inhibition that unfolds over seconds to minutes rather than the milliseconds of GABA-A gating. This slower time course suits its functions: reducing muscle tone and spasticity through inhibition in spinal circuits, and dampening reward urgency through presynaptic inhibition of dopamine release in limbic areas. As a metabotropic GPCR, baclofen's agonism at this receptor accounts for its clinical utility in spasticity and, increasingly, in reducing craving in alcohol use disorder.

abstract: The cholinergic receptor central to memory, attention, and the balance of thought itself. M1 engagement sharpens cognition in cortex and hippocampus; its blockade dims these processes, producing mental fog, memory lapses, and, over time, confusion. M1 activation also appears to quiet psychotic signalling without direct dopamine blockade.
presentation: Healthy M1 tone brings clear memory, focused attention, and emotional steadiness; its loss slides into mental fog, memory lapses, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and, in vulnerable people, confusion tipping into delirium.
effect: Excitatory: cognition; source of anticholinergic load
body: M1 receptors in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus support working memory, attention, and executive function through Gq-coupled phospholipase C signalling. Blockade, whether from tricyclic antidepressants, first-generation antipsychotics, or antihistamines, produces the anticholinergic syndrome: peripherally, dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and dilated pupils; centrally, mental fog, memory lapses, and, at higher load in vulnerable individuals, frank delirium. Cumulative anticholinergic burden over years is associated with accelerated cognitive decline. Selective M1 agonism, conversely, improves memory and attention, and may reduce psychotic symptoms through a mechanism independent of dopamine blockade; this is the rationale for xanomeline-trospium as a novel antipsychotic approach.

abstract: The fast acetylcholine channel that drives reinforcement and shapes attention. The α4β2 subtype carries the reward signal on dopamine neurons, making this receptor the substrate of dependence and craving. The α7 subtype supports sensory filtering: the suppression of irrelevant, repetitive stimuli to allow focused attention.
presentation: Healthy α4β2 tone underlies the capacity for reinforced learning and reward; its engagement produces a strong pull toward repetition, and its loss brings withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, and craving. α7 dysfunction weakens sensory gating, leaving the brain flooded with irrelevant stimuli and the person unable to filter noise.
body: α4β2 nicotinic receptors on mesolimbic dopamine neurons carry the reinforcing signal underlying reward learning. Chronic activation by nicotine produces upregulation of these receptors; in their absence, withdrawal emerges as irritability, dysphoria, and craving, reflecting the degree to which tonic nicotinic stimulation had been integrated into the reward circuit's baseline. The α7 subtype, expressed on prefrontal and hippocampal neurons, supports sensory gating: the suppression of redundant or irrelevant stimuli that allows attention to focus. Reduced α7 function impairs this filtering and is associated with the cognitive symptoms and P50 gating deficits seen in schizophrenia. Partial agonism at α4β2 (varenicline) reduces craving and blunts the reward response to smoking without producing the full reinforcing effect.

abstract: The brain's wakefulness dial. Central histamine sustains arousal and alertness throughout the day; it also helps restrain appetite. Blocking H1 brings heavy sedation; over time it drives weight gain through appetite disinhibition and reduced activity.
presentation: Active H1 signalling keeps a person awake, alert, and appetite-suppressed; blockade produces sedation within hours and, over weeks, progressive appetite increase and weight gain.
body: Histamine neurons in the tuberomammillary nucleus fire steadily throughout waking hours, sustaining cortical and thalamic arousal through H1 receptors. The same signalling restrains appetite through hypothalamic circuits. Blockade produces sedation within hours and, with sustained antagonism as occurs with many antipsychotics and antidepressants, progressive weight gain, driven by appetite disinhibition together with sedation-related inactivity and metabolic effects. The sedating properties are occasionally exploited therapeutically: mirtazapine and low-dose quetiapine are used partly for their H1 antagonism, where the same mechanism that is a side effect in one context is the intended effect in another.

abstract: The primary opioid receptor mediating analgesia, euphoria, and reward. Activation reduces pain signalling, produces sedation and emotional well-being, and engages the mesolimbic reward circuit. Repeated activation leads to tolerance and physical dependence; withdrawal produces dysphoria, autonomic hyperactivity, and craving. At supratherapeutic doses, respiratory depression is the critical risk.
presentation: μ-opioid engagement brings pain relief, warmth, emotional soothing, and pleasure; at higher doses, drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, and slowed breathing. Chronic engagement breeds tolerance and craving; withdrawal brings dysphoria, body aches, and sweating. Blunted baseline tone underlies some forms of anhedonia.
body: Endogenous opioid peptides (endorphins and enkephalins) act at μ receptors distributed throughout the central and peripheral nervous system to modulate pain, reward, and autonomic function. Activation produces analgesia, sedation, and well-being, through both direct inhibitory effects in pain pathways and disinhibition of mesolimbic dopamine neurons, where μ receptors silence GABAergic interneurons in the ventral tegmental area to release dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. At higher doses, μ-opioid agonism suppresses respiratory drive in the brainstem, making respiratory depression the primary risk of overdose. Repeated activation triggers receptor desensitization and downregulation: larger doses are required for equivalent analgesia (tolerance), and in the absence of expected agonism, withdrawal emerges, characterized by dysphoria, autonomic hyperactivity, and craving. Endogenous μ-opioid tone also contributes to baseline hedonic capacity; reduced signalling has been proposed as a mechanism in certain presentations of anhedonia, and partial agonism strategies are under investigation as adjunctive treatments in refractory depression.

abstract: The receptors that translate darkness into sleep and synchronize the body to the day-night cycle. MT1 primarily eases sleep onset and MT2 primarily shifts the circadian clock, though both are co-expressed in the suprachiasmatic nucleus and contribute to each. Together they read the melatonin signal from the pineal gland and tell the brain when night has arrived.
presentation: MT1 and MT2 signalling communicates darkness to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, triggering the shift toward sleep onset and aligning the internal clock to the external day-night cycle. MT1 activation promotes sleep onset; MT2 activation shifts circadian phase. The result is phase-aligned sleep rather than generalised sedation.
effect: Inhibitory: sets circadian phase and sleep onset
figure_caption: Fig. 22 · Gi coupling, the circadian clock
body: Melatonin, released from the pineal gland in darkness, circulates to the suprachiasmatic nucleus and binds MT1 and MT2 receptors in the brain's master circadian pacemaker. MT1 activation promotes sleep onset by reducing neuronal firing in wake-promoting circuits; MT2 activation advances or delays circadian phase, adjusting the clock to match the external light-dark cycle. Because the signal acts through endogenous circadian mechanisms rather than generalised sedation, it does not produce the tolerance, dependence, or residual impairment associated with benzodiazepines or z-drugs. Ramelteon (MT1/MT2 agonist) and tasimelteon (for non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder in blind individuals) exploit this mechanism clinically.

abstract: The newest sleep target, approached by withdrawing the signal that maintains wakefulness. Orexin neurons stabilize the brain in a continuous awake state; their loss is narcolepsy. Blocking OX1/OX2 reduces wake drive rather than producing generalised sedation, allowing sleep to emerge through normal mechanisms.
presentation: Healthy orexin tone sustains daytime wakefulness and a stable wake-sleep boundary; its loss is narcolepsy: daytime sleep attacks, fragmented night sleep, and emotion-triggered cataplexy. Blocking the signal reduces wake drive without producing generalised sedation.
figure_caption: Fig. 23 · Gq coupling, the wake switch
body: Orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus fire continuously throughout wakefulness, stabilizing arousal and maintaining a sharp wake-sleep boundary through excitatory projections to the locus coeruleus, raphe, and tuberomammillary nucleus. Their loss is narcolepsy with cataplexy: the inability to sustain wakefulness, with sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, reflecting orexin's role in suppressing REM motor atonia during waking hours. Dual orexin receptor antagonists (suvorexant, lemborexant) block both OX1 and OX2, reducing wake drive and facilitating sleep onset without the generalised CNS depression of benzodiazepines or z-drugs. The result is sleep with largely preserved architecture and lower rebound insomnia risk. Orexin replacement strategies, including OX2-selective agonists and intranasal orexin, are under investigation as approaches to narcolepsy that restore the missing arousal signal rather than compensating for it.
